launch-or-portland-washington-park.description: The free terraced rose garden at 400 SW Kingston Avenue is most colorful from late spring into fall; use the garden shuttle stop and expect steep paths between terraces.
The Oregon Zoo is a separately ticketed attraction beside Washington Park MAX station with its own hours, entrance, accessibility services, food, and parking zones.
Portland Japanese Garden is a separately ticketed hillside garden above the Rose Test Garden; use its Welcome Center and shuttle rather than climbing from a distant lot.
Hoyt Arboretum Visitor Center is the best orientation point for maps, restrooms, programs, and more than 12 miles of free arboretum trails.
World Forestry Center is beside the zoo and MAX station; museum exhibits, events, admission, and operating hours are independent of the outdoor park.
The Oregon Holocaust Memorial is a free, contemplative memorial reached from the northern park road and trail network; treat its artifacts and inscriptions respectfully.
The Vietnam Veterans of Oregon Memorial is a free landscaped memorial with a circular wall and accessible paths near the zoo and Hoyt Arboretum zone.
Washington Park Playground sits near the Rose Garden area with accessible play equipment, picnic facilities, and steep surrounding terrain.

launch-or-portland-forest-park.description: Lower Macleay is a popular transit-accessible start along Balch Creek with a larger parking area, ADA spaces, bike racks, and the route toward Stone House.
Stone House, often called Witch's Castle, is a roofless historic structure along Lower Macleay Trail; it is a trail landmark, not a staffed building or restroom.
The 30-mile natural-surface Wildwood Trail runs the length of Forest Park; use blue diamond markers, carry a map, and check closures before choosing a segment.
Leif Erikson Drive is a broad gravel multi-use route popular with runners and cyclists; the Thurman trailhead has very limited parking and bike racks.
The Wildwood/Pittock trailhead connects forest hiking with Pittock Mansion; parking is larger than many trailheads but the mansion and grounds keep separate rules.
Germantown Road accesses northern Wildwood and Leif Erikson routes; use the exact official lot because traffic and road shoulders make informal arrival unsafe.
Lower Saltzman offers one of Forest Park's larger parking areas and a gradual gravel road connection into the interior trail network.
The new Forest Park Entrance parking area provides access to Firelane 1; the future nature center is not yet an operating visitor facility.

launch-or-portland-tom-mccall-waterfront.description: Salmon Street Springs is the park's interactive fountain near SW Salmon Street; operation is seasonal and can pause for maintenance, weather, or water conditions.
The Japanese American Historical Plaza is a free memorial landscape at the park's north end with cherry trees, poetry stones, and Willamette views.
The Battleship Oregon Memorial mast stands near Oak Street as a historic landmark; surrounding lawns and paths may be occupied during large events.
Bill Naito Legacy Fountain and Plaza provide a newer accessible gathering and water-play destination near Saturday Market; check current fountain operation.
Waterfront Park Bowl is the broad southern lawn between Hawthorne Bridge and RiverPlace, used for recreation and major festivals that can fence or close the area.
South Breakwater Dock provides short-term active river access without services or overnight moorage; conditions and event restrictions can change quickly.
Ankeny Plaza and the Portland Saturday Market edge connect the waterfront to Old Town; market days create crowds, food vendors, street closures, and limited bike space.
The paved Willamette Greenway Trail runs through the park and is shared by walkers, runners, mobility devices, and bicycles; stay predictable in busy sections.

launch-or-portland-mt-tabor-park.description: The summit is the park's highest destination for city and mountain views, reached by road when open or by steep paved paths, stairs, and trails.
Historic open reservoirs form the visual heart of Mt. Tabor; enjoy them from paths and overlooks but do not enter fenced water infrastructure.
The outdoor amphitheater hosts concerts and events; pets are prohibited inside on concert days and event setups can restrict nearby paths.
The accessible playground is reached by a paved path with a moderate slope and sits below the summit among picnic and recreation areas.
The designated off-leash area is the only place for legal off-leash use; leash dogs throughout the rest of the park.
The summit-area picnic shelter is being rebuilt May through August 2026, with the shelter site and two nearby paths closed during construction.
Mt. Tabor Community Garden is an active allotment garden rather than a general picnic lawn; admire plots without entering or harvesting.
The PDX Adult Soapbox Derby uses the park's steep road course for its annual event, bringing road closures, crowds, noise, and limited parking.

launch-or-portland-laurelhurst-park.description: Firwood Lake is a spring-fed ornamental pond with ducks, turtles, fish, and seasonal duckweed; it is not a swimming or wading area.
The accessible playground has a ramp, transfer station, sensory elements, and adapted high-back swing, reached by a paved path from street parking.
The designated off-leash area follows detailed seasonal weekday and weekend hours; outside those windows dogs must remain leashed.
The shaded picnic grove has reservable sites and mature trees; reserve ahead for guaranteed group use or equipment beyond ordinary park rules.
The basketball court sits in the park's active recreation zone and is first-come unless reserved or programmed.
Marked pickleball courts share the active recreation area; bring equipment and expect wait times during popular hours.
Rhododendron Hill is a landscaped walking area best experienced during seasonal bloom, with curving paths and natural slopes.
The historic concert grove is an open lawn and gathering area rather than a staffed venue; programs and reservations can alter access.

launch-or-portland-cathedral-park.description: The Gothic arches beneath St. Johns Bridge create the park's signature viewpoint and event backdrop; bridge repair staging may change access.
The 2024 nature patch combines native and ornamental flowers, basalt, logs, and pollinator habitat near the upper bridge steps.
The amphitheater beneath the bridge hosts concerts, weddings, and festivals; event reservations can close seating and nearby lawns.
The public boat ramp and dock are open during park hours for active launching and short stays, with paid trailer parking and no overnight moorage.
A designated dog off-leash area sits near N Crawford Avenue with its own small free lot; dogs must be leashed elsewhere.
The paved lower waterfront path offers the park's flattest route, river views, docks, lawns, and connections between activity areas.
The river beach is informal, unsupervised shore access without lifeguards; currents, cold water, debris, and vessel traffic require caution.
The Wall of History and 1980 time capsule sit in the memorial garden; the capsule is intended to be opened in 2030.

launch-or-portland-peninsula-park.description: Portland's first public rose garden is a free formal landscape centered on a historic fountain, with peak bloom generally in warmer months.
The decorative rose-garden fountain and seasonal splash pad are separate water features; verify splash-pad operation before promising water play.
The historic community center provides classes, indoor facilities, and restrooms only during its own operating and program hours.
Portland's second-oldest playground is a neighborhood play destination near the community center, pool, lawns, and picnic areas.
The historically designated bandstand anchors the formal park and may be reserved for weddings, performances, or community events.
Peninsula Outdoor Pool is a seasonal, separately operated aquatic facility with admission, supervision rules, and a schedule that changes through summer.
The basketball court is part of the park's active recreation area and can be busy when the pool, center, or fields are programmed.
Lighted tennis courts operate until lights turn off at 10:00 p.m.; bring equipment and follow posted reservation or rotation rules.

launch-or-portland-powell-butte-nature-p.description: The visitor center is open Wednesday through Sunday 9:00 a.m.-3:00 p.m. and is the best first-stop for orientation and the accessible restroom.
The summit meadow offers broad Cascade views and little weather shelter; wind, heat, smoke, rain, and lightning can be more intense than in the forest.
Mountain View Trail crosses open summit terrain for expansive views; confirm trail-use designations and prepare for exposure.
Wildhorse Trail is part of the park's shared hiking, cycling, and equestrian network; yield according to posted trail etiquette.
Cedar Grove Trail enters shaded forest with natural surfaces, roots, mud, and seasonal debris that differ from the developed visitor-center routes.
Pipeline Lane is a broad utility corridor used to connect several loops; it can be exposed and less scenic but useful for navigation.
Goldfinch Trailhead is a neighborhood access with fewer facilities than the main entrance; arrive self-sufficient and park only where legal.
Ellis Street Trailhead reaches the south and west trail network from a neighborhood edge without the visitor-center services or main lot.
